articles.title: Will the Dems let Schumer & Jeffries sabotage the mandate?
articles.author: Zoe Alexandra
articles.content: A midterm blue tsunami, a total referendum on MAGA, and Democratic leaders are rushing to squander every bit of it. Rania Khalek sounds off on how Hakeem Jeffries, Chuck Schumer and “moderate” Democrats are working overtime to kill demands for Medicare for All, an end to the war on Iran, and a cutoff of weapons to Israel – before the new Congress is even sworn in Khalek explains why freshman insurgents like Claire Valdez, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Melat Kiros won’t automatically fall in line behind Jeffries for House speaker – even as AOC keeps backing him – starting with the AIPAC money behind him. Meanwhile, incoming Rep. Don Leonard says senior House Democrats are threatening to make his life “a living hell” for attaching conditions to his vote: a vote to end Citizens United and an end to the war on Iran. And Schumer’s grip is slipping: the 600,000-member Machinists union turned against him this week, and Sen. Chris Van Hollen says he’s open to taking his job as Senate majority leader. But the establishment gears keep turning: as Majority Democrats meet in Denver to shape the 2028 platform, corporate media is piling on universal healthcare. Khalek breaks down why the self-styled “party of the people” is so afraid of Medicare for All — and who cashes in when it stays off the table. Khalek says the first test comes with the government funding deadline on December 11. Will Dems side with the voters who just handed them a mandate, or the donors who paid for their seats? #breakthroughnews

articles.title: A thank you note from the organisers of the 2026 Historical Materialism London Conference
articles.author: Panagiotis Sotiris
articles.content: A huge thanks to all the participants in the 2026 Historical Materialism London conference. The biggest so far with: Four full days of panels Around 1,600 participants in total 317 panels 22 parallel sessions at peak times 40 participants for the PGR conference on 4 November We would like to express our gratitude that you all came here and brought your theoretical and political work to share and debate to find collective ways how to think and act as Marxists in the broadest sense of the term in this world and conjuncture. We would like to thank you for this huge commitment to travel (some of you from very far, at great expense, negotiating highly punitive border regimes), to take time off work, interrupt organising work, write papers whilst juggling a million other demands, in order to come here to London for these 4 very intense days. So many of you already shared with us how you gained a lot of hope, inspiration and energy from the rich and diverse presentations and the conversations you had – and how this conference serves as an anchor that reminds us that we’re not alone with the convictions from which we think and act, even if it can easily feel like that in our everyday lives and work environments. The death of our comrade, friend and co-editor Peter D. Thomas four weeks ago was a huge blow to us, but it’s a testament to our collective that we found a way to go through this and it is hugely important to carry on this work that was so central to Peter’s theoretical and political commitment. In the months that come, we will honour his legacy in many ways, up to and including organising a series of sessions on his work during next year’s conference. The success of this conference is an expression of the continuous pertinence of critical Marxist theory in these times of reaction, genocide, impending extinction, but also of resistance movements and shows that it continues to create new resources of hope. It also underlines the importance of trenchant, insightful and comradely debate among Marxists as the indispensable condition for the urgently needed new emancipatory projects. Moreover, this attendance was yet another demonstration of support and solidarity for the broader HM project, and, from our part we reiterate our commitment to improving and expanding it. There is not better proof of the growing importance of the HM project than the increasing number of HM conferences internationally. articles.title: Sudanese Communist Party demands release of arrested member
articles.author: Nicholas Mwangi
articles.content: The Sudanese Communist Party has condemned the arrest of Ahmed Babiker, known as Jughraf, a party member in the South Blue Nile region, and demanded his immediate release or that he be brought before a competent court. In a press statement, the party said Babiker was arrested by the security unit in Ed Damazin on Thursday, November 5, at the Agadi exit checkpoint. He was traveling by motorcycle with a colleague, Haq-Allah, who was not detained and was subsequently released. According to the statement, the two were heading to a camp for internally displaced persons to undertake a construction project. The work involved building traditional shelters, known as karanks, using bricks and straw. The party said Babiker had since been denied access to visitors. It condemned the circumstances surrounding his arrest and raised concerns about its legal basis. “The arrest lacks any legal basis other than the emergency laws that have remained in effect since the early years of the war,” the statement said. The party’s South Blue Nile branch reiterated its condemnation of the arrest, demanding that the authorities account for his detention and respect his legal rights. Arrest amid extended state of emergency The arrest comes amid an extended state of emergency in Blue Nile. In September 2026, the region’s governor, Ahmed al-Omda Badi, renewed emergency measures for three months, granting the army, police and intelligence authorities’ powers to take measures deemed necessary to maintain security. Read more: Sudanese Communist Party leader arrested by military intelligence It is not the first time the party has been targeted in the city. Since the civil war broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) on April 15, 2023, the Sudanese Communist Party (SCP) has faced numerous attacks. In August 2023, months after the war began, military intelligence raided the Communist Party’s office in Ed Damazin during an event marking its 77th anniversary and detained more than 20 people.

articles.title: Anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Eisenkot tasked with forming new Israeli government
articles.author: Aseel Saleh
articles.content: Israeli President Isaac Herzog officially tasked the leader of the anti-Netanyahu bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, with forming the next government, on Sunday, November 8. This came after Eisenkot secured 67 Knesset recommendations (combining 48 from his own coalition and 19 from Arab-led parties) surpassing the 61-seat threshold needed to form a government. After receiving the mandate, the designated candidate has a 28-day window (plus a potential 14-day extension granted by the Israeli president) to assemble a majority coalition in order to form a government with a minimum of 61 lawmakers. In the meantime, Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister until the new government takes office, as per Israel’s Basic Law. Read more: Final vote count for Israeli elections yields no clear winner Eisenkot’s four core principles for his proposed government Gadi Eisenkot set out four major principles for his proposed coalition government as follows. Recognition of Israel as a Jewish and “democratic” state Under this principle, all parties willing to join the coalition would be required to recognize Israel’s identity as the national home of the Jewish people. This requirement has long been a point of friction for the Arab parties, currently holding 19 Knesset seats. The principle also stipulates that coalition members commit to upholding Israel’s democratic institutions and the rule of law. This, in turn, may prevent far-right and ultra-Orthodox factions from joining the coalition, given their recent support for judicial reforms aimed at limiting oversight of the government. Embracing the values of the Declaration of Independence Eisenkot invoked Israel’s foundational 1948 Declaration of Independence , which purportedly calls for creating a state that represents a safe home for Jewish people, while maintaining a democracy based on peaceful coexistence, freedom, and equal rights for everyone. The principle ignited controversy as it underscored deep divisions over Israel’s national identity, secular–religious boundaries, and political calculations needed to maintain the balance of power. Mandatory military service for all Israeli citizens In accordance with this principle, Eisenkot demands that all Israeli citizens – regardless of their gender – perform either mandatory military service or an approved civilian-national alternative. This principle sparked debate because it challenges Israel’s delicate social, religious, and political balance. Ultra-Orthodox Haredi communities view military conscription as a major threat to their full-time Torah study and religious lifestyle. As a result, their leaders consider draft exemptions an absolute prerequisite for remaining in coalition governments. Concurrently, secular and mainstream Israelis argue that exempting Ultra-Orthodox citizens from military service violates the principle of equality by making non-religious citizens bear an unfair share of military risks during wartime shortages. This stance was supported by Israeli Supreme Court rulings that invalidated the exemptions. On the other hand, Arab leaders view the extension of mandatory national or community service to Arab citizens as inequitable as long as structural inequalities remain unaddressed. Recognizing Hamas as a “terrorist” organization, and committing to dismantle it All the Arab parties in Israel’s Knesset refrained from publicly endorsing this precondition. Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas expressed an “unequivocal” private position supporting the disarmament of Hamas. However, he avoids making a public declaration, citing safety concerns for his family, precarious ideological positions within the Islamic Movement with which he is affiliated, and a practical need to remain neutral enough to act as a mediator while preserving support from his Palestinian constituency. Meanwhile, the Joint List refuses the requirement on political and national grounds, arguing that labeling Hamas as a “terrorist group” would delegitimize broader Palestinian national aspirations, and justify Israel’s ongoing military operations in the Gaza Strip. Netanyahu slams assignment of Eisenkot, calls for unity government In protest to Herzog’s decision, Israeli Caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu posted a video , calling for the formation of a unity government. “Now unity. Two days ago, I called for the formation of a unity government. It is the need of the hour. Do you know why it is the need of the hour? First and foremost, because it is impossible to form a government that includes or is dependent on supporters of Hamas,” Netanyahu said. “You cannot fight Iran and its various proxies within radical Islam, if your own government relies on supporters of that very same radical Islam. Therefore, a unity government is an absolute necessity,” he asserted.

articles.title: Bible, Family, and Property: Who is Paraguay’s New President, Pedro Alliana?
articles.content: On Friday, October 6, Pedro Alliana was ushered in as president of Paraguay. His ascension followed the impeachment of President Santiago Peña amid the Ueno Bank crisis. Members of Javier Milei’s administration in Argentina applauded Alliana’s arrival to power. According to an Argentine official who spoke to the news channel TN, the new Paraguayan president is “even further to the right and closer to Milei’s ideas than Santiago Peña was.” This assessment is supported by recent statements from the 52-year-old politician, who built his political career within the traditional Colorado Party and, more recently, has aligned himself with religious-based rhetoric and international conservative leaders. During the 2023 presidential campaign, Alliana declared that his party stood for the teachings of God and the Bible, as well as for life, family, and private property. He presented his party as a bulwark against abortion and what is termed “gender ideology.” A former governor of the Ñeembucú department, a member of parliament, and a former president of both the Chamber of Deputies and the Colorado Party, Alliana assumed the vice presidency in 2023 as part of the ticket with Peña. Alliana’s national prominence emerged within “Honor Colorado,” a faction of the Colorado Party led by former president Horacio Cartes, who governed Paraguay from 2013 to 2018. Cartes is a businessman with interests in the financial, tobacco, and agricultural sectors. He solidified his influence over the party and served as the primary architect behind the election of both Peña and Alliana. His administration pursued policies of economic liberalization and expanded partnerships with the private sector. The Colorado Party supported the dictatorship of Alfredo Stroessner (1954–1989) and has governed Paraguay since 1947, with the exception of the period between 2008 and 2012, when Fernando Lugo served as president. In 2023, during Joe Biden’s term, Cartes was the target of financial sanctions by the United States, following accusations of corruption and the payment of bribes to officials. He denies any wrongdoing. The sanctions were lifted by the Donald Trump administration in October 2025, a decision publicly celebrated by Alliana. The defense of religious agendas was already present in the rhetoric of the new Paraguayan president back in 2018, when he led the Colorado Party. During an event held by the Republican Institute for Strategic Policy, a party-affiliated organization that adopted the motto “God, Homeland, and Family,” Alliana declared: “We say no to abortion, and we defend the fundamental values ​​we hold as a nation: our history and our Christian principles.” This narrative also featured prominently in the 2023 campaign. Alliana claimed that foreign nations intended to introduce abortion and so-called “gender ideology” into Paraguay, describing the Colorado Party as a bulwark in defense of life and the family. That same year, he called for the elimination of an educational cooperation agreement between Paraguay and the European Union, alleging that foreign funds could be used to finance gender-related content in schools. The European Union denied having any influence over the Paraguayan school curriculum and clarified that the funding was not contingent upon the adoption of any specific educational content. A study by the International Institute for Democracy and Electoral Assistance (International IDEA) identified similarities between the propaganda used in the Peña-Alliana campaign and the materials disseminated by Jair Bolsonaro against Lula in 2022. According to the research, both campaigns employed comparisons over abortion, gender, censorship, and public safety to attack their opponents. Anti-communism also appears in statements made by the Colorado Party leader. In January 2022, Alliana celebrated his party’s return to power in 1947, describing the event as a popular reaction against communism. Paraguayan historians have challenged this interpretation, pointing out that the political shift actually followed a self-coup by General Higinio Morínigo. In recent years, Alliana has strengthened ties with members of the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump. In August 2026, he met with Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Undersecretary Christopher Landau in the United States. In an interview with the Argentine outlet Infobae, he stated that relations between the two countries were experiencing “an extraordinary moment” and might well be at their historical peak. Alliana expressed support for the “Shield of the Americas,” a Trump-era initiative aimed at consolidating U.S. hegemony in the region, with an official agenda focused on regional security cooperation and combating organized crime. He also voiced support for Pax Silica, a U.S. program focused on developing supply chains for critical technologies and minerals. During the visit, the two nations signed a memorandum on civil nuclear cooperation, with Alliana highlighting the potential for exploring uranium reserves within Paraguayan territory. Military cooperation was further expanded through a Status of Forces Agreement signed with the United States in December 2025 and approved by the Paraguayan Congress in March 2026. The treaty allows for the temporary presence of U.S. military personnel and civilian staff in Paraguay, grants them immunity, and authorizes the United States to exercise criminal jurisdiction over them while on Paraguayan soil. In Argentina, the new Paraguayan president established direct contact with Santiago Caputo, one of Javier Milei’s key political advisors. The two met at the Casa Rosada in December 2025. Afterward, Alliana publicly thanked the Argentine strategist for gifting him a copy of El Monje, a book detailing his own political career. Another diplomatic meeting took place with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Alliana visited Israel in October 2026, where he met with the leader and reaffirmed Paraguay’s support for the Israeli government. In an interview with The Jerusalem Post, he stated that his country would maintain its strategic alliance with Israel, regardless of the political costs. He also defended Israel’s right to “protect its territory” and advocated for the expansion of bilateral cooperation in the fields of security and technology. In domestic policy, Alliana supported a reform of the Paraguayan public-sector pension system, which sparked protests by teachers in 2026. The proposal introduced changes to retirement rules and employee contributions. Following union mobilization, the then-vice president took part in negotiations that led to modifications in the bill. Before Peña’s fall, Alliana had been preparing to run for the presidency in 2028. His candidacy caused a rift with Cartes, who withdrew his support for Alliana’s electoral ambitions. Alliana received backing from Colorado Party governors and lawmakers, while Peña had supported his own succession by Alliana. According to Cony Oviedo, a leader of Paraguay’s Coordination of Organizations of Rural and Indigenous Working Women, Peña’s replacement does not represent a shift in the power structure. “The problem isn’t solved by the departure of a single president,” she told Brasil de Fato. She argued that the Colorado Party will remain in control of the country without taking responsibility for the crisis. Alliana was also implicated in the Ueno Bank scandal. The then-vice president confirmed that he held a certificate of deposit worth 4 billion guaranis (approximately $640,000) at the bank. The Chamber of Deputies rejected an impeachment motion against him by 48 votes to 30 while approving the impeachment process against Peña. The existence of the investment does not, in itself, prove involvement in the irregularities under investigation. Peña’s removal, which was supported by Cartes, accelerated Alliana’s rise to power, but it also altered his electoral plans. Under the Paraguayan Constitution, he is required to serve out the remainder of the term until August 2028 and is ineligible to run for presidential reelection.

articles.title: Spain: From occupation to general strike
articles.author: Thomas Hummel
articles.content: W hen the Policía Nacional of Madrid raided María del Carmen Abascal’s home to forcibly remove the 87-year-old from her apartment of over 70 years, they undoubtedly did not expect to kindle a nationwide explosion for dignified housing. The housing company Urbagestión had purchased her property and tripled her rent to more than her entire monthly state pension. As these pigs told the old woman and the protesters who had gathered to defend her that they were “just doing their job,” they certainly did not suspect that this would be the spark that would ignite a hot autumn in Madrid and across all of the Spanish state. After getting the call from the tenants’ union, hundreds of activists came to defend Maricarmen’s home from the police on the night of September 23. The police brutally arrested protesters, forcibly removed the disabled tenant, and brought her to a hospital. Three days later, 300,000 people marched through the streets of Madrid to protest against both this eviction and the widespread unsustainable state of housing across Spain. As they often do, the demonstration ended in Puerta del Sol, the city center, a bit like Times Square, though less garish. Instead of dispersing, however, thousands of protesters occupied the square, demanding the return of Maricarmen to her home, a moratorium on evictions, and a law for indefinite contracts with automatic renewal. Maricarmen’s case may be cruel, but it is not exceptional. In 2025, there were 24,540 evictions across the Spanish state, with nearly seven thousand in Catalonia and 2,267 in Madrid. The very same day that Maricarmen was expelled from her home, another eviction took place a handful of miles away in the working-class suburb of Vallecas, where a father and son were thrown out onto the streets. Earlier in September, the eviction of a mother of two in Barcelona led to her suicide. The first quarter of 2026 saw 4,005 evictions across the Spanish state. On average, renters spend 50 percent of their income on housing, causing the question to become the most important political issue for people across the nation , according to a recent state-sponsored poll. As Alicia del Río and Valeria Racu, two spokespeople of Madrid’s powerful tenants’ union, “Sindicato de Inquilinas” (SdI), recently wrote in El País , “there are moments when thousands of small histories suddenly converge into History with a capital H.” This is one of those moments. The seed is falling on ground during a political juncture where it is likely to be particularly fecund. It’s important to note that this movement has gone beyond a simple protest for housing and has become an indictment of the entire political system. The volatility of the Spanish situation is not unique. It is emblematic of the larger international political situation: an economic state of affairs that is increasingly untenable for ordinary people, the failure of the new social democratic progressivism to address this, new social movements that are beginning to succeed in reaching traditional working class sectors, and the long and grim shadow of far-right electoral success looming with menace over all. This article will trace some specifics of recent history that led to this social explosion in the Spanish state and plot some possible futures for the Spanish Left. It will then connect this social explosion to the broader political moment internationally to help draw out the character of the current period, and pose strategies for the Left appropriate to this character. There is now an opportunity to forge new bonds between social movements and the working class. Backdrop to a social explosion To begin with the economy, recent years have found Spain in a contradictory position. On paper, the economy is doing modestly well, especially relative to the rest of the developed world and its European neighbors in particular. Its GDP is projected to grow 2.1 percent in 2026 , triple the predicted growth rate in the broader Eurozone. It is dramatically outpacing the other “Big Four” EU countries, Germany, France, and Italy, all of which are experiencing near-stagnation. Yet, this boom has been driven almost exclusively by extensive growth, by adding new jobs to the economy without improving their productivity (which has flatlined in the country) or the compensation and working conditions of those jobs. The growth in GDP masks a more complex reality where real wages have declined to roughly 7 percent below their 2020 levels , 14.1 percent of employed Spanish workers are unable to adequately heat their homes during the winter, 10 percent have fallen behind on housing-related bills, and 25.7 percent of the population is classified as “at risk of poverty or social exclusion.” This stagnation has fallen especially hard on young people, who see themselves increasingly condemned to a life of precarity and struggle. Spain’s youth unemployment rate sits at 22.8 percent . While this is down from its post-2008 peak of 55.44 percent in 2013 , most of the jobs that have been created are precarious, in tourism and the service sectors. A huge percentage of the youth pursue university degrees that no longer guarantee economic stability as they did for their parents. The housing market is where the divide between generations is the most stark. The older generations benefited from a market where housing was relatively proportional to wages. Today that connection is completely severed. Only 14.5 percent of people under 30 years old live independently, and 85.5 percent still live with their parents. Average rent for a solo apartment would consume 98.7 percent of the average young worker’s salary . Meanwhile, the rich across the Spanish state are doing very well for themselves. In 2022 , the top 1 percent accumulated 26-27 percent of total new wealth, while the top 10 percent held 60 percent of the country’s total wealth. The bottom 50 percent of the country held only 7 percent of total wealth. In 2025, CEO compensation rose 16 percent, while average salaries rose only 3.6 percent . As was the case across the world, all sorts of divides were exacerbated by the pandemic, and wealth inequality spiked. Corporate profits shot up, going from their historical baseline of 10.5 percent to 13.9 percent , particularly in the energy, banking, and food retail sectors, while wage recovery from the pandemic has stalled completely. This social explosion comes after eight years of “the most progressive government in history,” a social democratic alliance led by PSOE, the traditional center-left social democratic party. PSOE governed in successive coalitions with Podemos—the young reformist project that filled the void left by the retreat of 15M, the “Indignados” upsurge in 2011—and then with Sumar, which could perhaps best be summed up as Podemos without the hope. Rents have risen 45 percent in the last 8 years , and according to SdI, there have been an estimated 300,000 evictions during the past eight years of this “progressive” government. To add to the dissatisfaction are the slew of scandals affecting PSOE and Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez’s inner circle, the increased military spending since the war in Ukraine, and the failure of this government to keep its promise to repeal the 2015 “ Ley Mordaza ”—an authoritarian law that allows fines for unannounced protests and disrespect toward police officers, broader powers for police searches, and legal protection for immediate expulsions of migrants attempting to cross the border. The left organizations are also increasingly discredited on the national scene. Podemos reached its peak electoral success in 2015, when it secured 20.7 percent of the vote, but has since fallen to an estimated 3.7 percent of total national support. Stepping into its place and retreating politically, Sumar won 12.3 percent of the vote in the July 2023 general election, but its support has since declined to an estimated 5.7 percent across the country. The contradictions of entering a coalition government and having to take responsibility for the disappointment with the limitations of the reformist project have drained these organizations of the vitality they once had. They continue to limp along, but mostly in a hollow state, with low levels of active membership. As across much of the world, the crisis, combined with the failure of the institutional left, has sent people looking for scapegoats and into the hands of the far right. Previous to the eviction of Maricarmen, the defining features of Spanish politics were the cascading scandals in PSOE and the mass crossing of migrants at the Spanish North African enclave at Ceuta . Spanish imperialism in North Africa has long been a defining feature of the Spanish far right, nearly as central to its raison d’etre as its opposition to the regional nationalisms. This, combined with fascist-adjacent VOX’s virulent anti-immigrant racism, frames the crisis as an “invasion” against which Spanish Christendom must be defended, as in the days of the medieval “Reconquista.” VOX poll numbers have surged to 18 percent. Before Maricarmen’s eviction and the calling of new elections for November 29, it was near certain that VOX and an increasingly Trumpified Partido Popular would take power after the August 2027 elections. Now, however, the housing movement has recaptured this energy and is the principal actor setting the national agenda. One of the far-right slogans read, “the problem is the invaders,” and the housing movement has cleverly flipped that into “the problem is the investors.” During the period of “the most progressive government in history,” the organizations of the extra-parliamentary Left also accumulated forces and developed power. This was particularly true for the national network of tenants’ unions informally led by Madrid’s Sindicato de Inquilinas, which, starting in 2017, slowly began to accumulate power and become a central pole of attraction for the Left. What seemed like a spontaneous explosion was as much a result of sudden rage as the nine years of slow and tedious groundwork, building power neighborhood by neighborhood throughout the Spanish state. It is indicative of this groundwork that Maricarmen was in touch with SdI before her eviction. Sindicato de Inquilinas is a very politically sophisticated organization with deep roots in the anticapitalist left. Most of its core cadre come from these traditions, whether socialist or anarchist. These cadre have absorbed, through study and personal experience, a lot of the key lessons of the past cycles of struggle and have adapted themselves accordingly, with great success. It has grown around a few core demands : Rent reduction of 50 percent Public expropriation of empty housing and housing owned by vulture funds A return of all tourist apartments to the rental market Indefinite contracts without rate increases Outlawing of the eviction-for-hire groups (Desokupa thugs) End of all evictions End of housing speculation Expand public housing stock and dissolve SAREB (vulture state bank, formed in 2012 to clean up the country’s financial sector following the 2008 real estate and banking crisis). In a certain sense, SdI is a united front of the radical Left that has successfully broken out of the social backwaters we have long been stuck in, and has reached broader layers of the working class. It’s interesting to read sober reflections on the experiences of the Left through the last decade from members of the group. In a recent article in “El Salto,” members of SdI compared the differences between 15M in 2011 and the uprising today, reflecting on hierarchy and organization and specifically citing Vicent Bevins’ If We Burn . This is an organization that is learning, that is engaged with the past with an eye toward the future. As a united front organization, it is radically uneven and contains a lot of anarchist and reformist tendencies (sometimes in the same people). Revolutionary socialists have been and need to continue to work within the organization to pull new members to the left and pull the core cadre toward genuine revolutionary socialist positions, arguing for the need for specific revolutionary organizations in addition to the broad organs of the class. After the encampment By September 29, six days after Maricarmen’s eviction, 1,200 tents were set up in Puerta del Sol. A small community emerged, with duties distributed, voting assemblies, and political organizing and discussion happening everywhere. Within a week, over 60 demonstrations took place throughout the Spanish state, and other encampments began to fill the centers of major cities. On October 3, an estimated 500,000 people flooded the streets of Madrid to demand change from the national government. The encampments around the country have had to fend off attempts by far-right street thugs to violently break them up. As early as the third of October, a fascist group, Indignados por España, tried to break up the encampment in Sol. In Oviedo, in the province of Asturias, four members of far-right groups were arrested for assaulting people at the local encampment after shouting Nazi slogans and giving the fascist salute. On the highly nationalist “Día de la Hispanidad” (Spanish Heritage Day), hundreds of far-right sympathizers, mostly quite young, approached the encampment , giving fascist salutes and singing the fascist anthem “Cara al Sol” and chanting “rojo muerto, abono para mi huerto,” “a dead red is fertilizer for my garden.” Responding to the demands of the housing movement, Pedro Sánchez’s cabinet approved two emergency decree-laws: one suspending evictions until 2030, the other guaranteeing indefinite rental contracts. Under Spanish law, these had to be ratified by the Congreso de los Diputados within thirty days. The expectation was that the former would pass, the latter would fail, and that these crumbs would be enough to appease the housing movement. SdI was very clear , however, that “if indefinite contracts are not approved, this country is governed by the housing speculators.” When the time came for a vote on October 2, Sánchez’s parliamentary majority fell apart. The bourgeois Catalan nationalist party “Junts” refused to support either piece of legislation, and the legislation failed as a result. The tenants’ union began to call for a general strike, and Sánchez, recognizing the shifting winds and the possibility of riding this housing discontent to an extended tenure, called for snap elections for 29 November. With Parliament dissolved, the previous legislative measures were raised again by the government almost unchanged as two new decree laws, published on October 7, which now have been ratified Permanent Deputation, the reduced body of 69 deputies that stand in for Congress until a new one is elected. The first decree contains an eviction ban that lasts until 2030, a 2 percent cap on rent increases through the end of 2027, compensation for tenants if landlords do not extend contracts, restrictions on property purchases by vulture funds, landlord tax breaks, and a €10 billion “help to buy” program offering up to €50,000 in interest-free loans for first-time homebuyers. The second decree makes rental contracts renew automatically. Both are provisionally in force, but they lapse if they aren’t ratified by November 13. The vote is scheduled for the 12, and the first is expected to pass, but the second, the heart of the movement’s demands, is likely to fail since the PNV, the Basque Nationalist Party, opposes it. Even if they do pass, the next government could repeal them, and Sánchez is counting on this to frighten voters into keeping him in power. Meanwhile, the movement in the streets secured an important victory by forcing Maricarmen’s landlord to sign a new lease with her on October 2nd. Yet tragically, on October 7, the day before she was set to sign the new lease, Maricarmen suddenly died, prompting new demonstrations and memorials accusing the state and the vulture funds of social murder. The encampment itself has followed a different trajectory from its 2011 predecessor. After the decrees of October 2, the assembly at Sol voted to stay indefinitely, but SdI deliberately scaled back its presence to prepare for the general strike. What remained in Sol held out until the police cleared it on November 3, removing 334 people and arresting 2. The general strike The housing movement has not been the only protest movement rocking Madrid in recent weeks. The teacher’s unions (at the forefront of working class militancy, as is often the case), went out on indefinite strike on October 14, demanding a lower maximum number of classes per week, smaller class sizes, and a raise of €600 per month. The demands are inseparable from housing since one analysis recently found that a newly hired teacher in Madrid would have to spend 65.4 percent of their net salary on rent. The social and political ties between these two movements are deep, and on the first night of the strike, thousands of teachers marched to Sol to join the encampment. Madrid doctors also walked out on strike on October 28, with demands that overlap with Madrid’s longstanding public health movement, Marea Blanca. Within weeks, three sectoral struggles over housing, education, and health have converged against the same regional government headed by the Trumpist Isabel Ayuso. Sindicato de Inquilinas had built enough power and legitimacy for itself that it was able to influence the labor movement, acting as the key liaison between the movement in the streets and the major unions. It had built sufficient credibility for itself that it could realistically call for a general strike. The left-wing unions were easy enough to bring on board, but SdI’s ability to meet with the heavily bureaucratic CCOO (Comisiones Obreras) and UGT (Unión General de Trabajadores), the largest and most prominent labor unions in the country, and pull them into calling a general strike for November 11, shows the gravity that the tenants union now carries. The strike has also gained the support of the regional nationalist unions like the Galician CIG and the Basque ELA and LAB who are adding their own set of demands related to regional autonomy. Inevitably, the general strike will be of an extremely hybrid character. Like many large bureaucratic unions, the political method of the CCOO and UGT over the last decades has been aptly defined as “traicionar luchando,” “to betray while fighting,” although the CCOO in particular has a strong Marxist-inspired left wing in its ranks. These unions did not want this strike. They have been the determined partisans of the “social peace” that has defined the neoliberal age, “ministers without portfolio,” as one analysis astutely referred to them. They will seek to limit the horizon of the struggle to within boundaries they can manage, essentially using it as a rally to keep a left coalition in power (a possible secondary aim being to demonstrate their willingness to fight to an incoming right-wing government). The fact that the general strike is limiting itself in advance to a single day shows the extent to which it is built on a compromise with a union bureaucracy that is willing to sacrifice effectiveness for security. On the other hand, the general strike is an enormous opportunity for the anticapitalist Left to work in solidarity with a huge sector of strategically important workers in the CCOO and the UGT, including in the significant but forgotten manufacturing sector (it’s often overlooked that Spain has the second largest auto manufacturing industry in Europe). Through the general strike, the working class gains self-confidence through the practical experience of mass united action. It is a concrete lesson of the power of working-class united action. As Brais Fernández recently put it , revolutionaries must “construct the general strike in order to go beyond it.” Reformism always has a vampiric relationship to movements in the streets. We saw this in the U.S. when the movement for Palestine breathed new life into DSA reformism without acknowledging this debt. In the Spanish state, reformism found rejuvenation through the militancy of Los Indignados in 2011. Yet despite this limited truth, the overall dynamic is more complex and dialectical. The movement from below learns not to cede the space it has conquered to reformism, while, to try to find yet another rebirth, sections of the reformist bloc are forced to strategically adopt more militant tactics to keep the faith of its base and to mask its essence, which is betrayal. This in turn allows for revolutionaries to reach larger sections of the class who still maintain faith in these institutions, or do not yet see a credible alternative. The revolutionary Left must continually contest the social democrats’ and union bureaucrats’ hegemony within the movement around the strike. SdI is spearheading an initiative that will leverage its geographic implantation—to form neighborhood strike assemblies, mass democratic spaces where strategy and tactics for the movement can be debated. By early November there were 1,340 strike committees across 108 cities and SdI had created a digital platform for people to find info on their local assembly. These bodies can coordinate their intervention in the strike, collectively raising demands that will pull the class toward them and away from the reformists. These may include, as Anticapitalistas suggests, a 50 percent rent reduction and linking rent to 20 percent of salary . These are spaces revolutionaries can work inside to push them to the left and make them permanent so that they can serve as tools of organization in coming struggles. The November 29 election The progressive bloc is seeking to use the movements in the streets to turn the elections from a referendum on Sánchez into a referendum on housing. The right wants to talk about everything but housing (and economic issues more generally). They want the focus to be on corruption in PSOE, immigration, and the culture war. Over all of this hope and self-activity hangs the sobering executioner’s axe of the elections on November 29. The polls at this point are inconsistent, with the majority indicating a likely PP/VOX victory, but the more weighty (in both breadth and rigor) state-sponsored Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas (CIS) polls suggesting a victory for a PSOE-led coalition. As CIS has a history of overestimating the weight of PSOE in the past, it’s perhaps possible to say that a PP/VOX coalition is the most likely outcome of the elections, though this is far from guaranteed. The promise of housing reform may not be enough to undo the last eight years of disillusion and disappointment. The desperate, false hope that, if the progressive Left was unable to deliver, then perhaps, somehow, the right’s program of anti-immigration and austerity will be able to improve living conditions for ordinary people—this could cause PP/VOX to prevail. Other polling bears this out . A poll conducted by 40dB for El País y la Cadena SER found that two out of three people support limiting the cost of rent, even if this reduces profits for landlords. 55 percent of VOX and PP voters said they would support these measures. Another poll published by elDiario showed that 73 percent of people support a general strike to solve the problem of housing, including 61 percent of PP voters, and 63 percent of VOX voters. This shows that what draws the majority of these voters right is not conviction, but desperation, and that many of these people could be pulled left with the appearance of a credible alternative. This situation is illustrative of how deeply the crisis is hollowing out the center and heightening social contradictions. VOX will almost certainly gain its largest showing, with all polls putting them just south of 20 percent. Their previous peak was 15 percent in the 2019 elections. The Francoist regime, still within living memory for many, has long acted as a brake on the far-right’s growth, but the generational turnover is beginning to seriously weaken that brake’s effectiveness. VOX’s influence on politics also goes beyond their numerical results in elections. They have been able to pull PP toward increasingly far-right positions to the point where the party could be justifiably described as Trumpist or at least Trumpifying. If a PP/VOX coalition wins, the state will impose brutal austerity (including pension reform) and anti-migrant policies at the same moment when the social movements and working class activity are at their highest point in decades. This could either lead to a sustained period of heightened struggle, a test of strength in which the anticapitalist Left will continue to make inroads, or a period of defeats severe enough to force the working-class movement onto the back foot. On the other hand, if CIS is right and victory is delivered to a PSOE-led coalition, the country would be set for another period largely similar to the past eight years, though with some important changes. While the coalition will no longer depend on the Catalan nationalist party, Junts, the strength of the Left within the coalition will be considerably weakened. In 2023, the Left ran on a shared ticket that won 12.3 percent of the vote and 31 seats in the legislature. Now in 2026, exacerbated by the failure of Podemos to reach an agreement with Sumar and the other small left parties, they are slated to win only 9 percent and 10 total seats. Showing how the far-right learns from each other internationally, the leader of PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo is applying the Trump playbook by already casting doubts on the legitimacy of the elections, raising specters of mass fraud that have no basis in reality. This is something else with which the Left will have to contend in case of a PSOE victory. Regardless of who wins (“gobierne quien gobierne” is the slogan in the streets, which repurposed it from the movement for public health in Madrid), there are certain features of the moment for the Left that will remain the same. In contrast to the period following 15M, when the new reformist Left surged into the space opened and then vacated by the youth movement, the new reformism is on life support, and the movement has learned some of the lessons that allowed the institutional Left to channel its energy into a reformist project. This does not mean that the reformist Left will not find a second life, but as it stands currently the movement in the streets looks strong enough that it can resist cannibalization by reformism. Reforging the bonds between movement and class It’s worth taking a look at some of the central differences between 15M and the current movement to think about how the moment has changed and what it means for the left. 2011 was still early days in the disintegration of neoliberalism. Neoliberalism’s onslaught successfully broke the bonds between the Left and the class, turning the Left into a marginal subculture, with rites and rituals increasingly alien to the broad working classes. The unions adopted a strategy of keeping their heads down to survive the onslaught, and were able by doing so—though sometimes just barely—to keep the living standards of their members above a certain level. Now the process of the disintegration of the neoliberal order is in a more advanced phase. The ruling class is torn among itself, and is unable to present a coherent project that the majority of society can rally behind. The only way for the ruling class to continue to accumulate capital is by trying to extract further concessions from an already exhausted population. The unions can no longer keep living standards above a certain level for their members, even if they promise the state they will behave. The movements of the squares in the 2010–2013 wave of protests were precisely the expressions of this separation between the movements and the class. Previous to the neoliberal age, this level of social discontent would have been channeled immediately into general strikes, which, in certain cases, would pose the question of social revolution. The movements of the squares floundered into dead ends due to this separation, because they had not yet built the organizational infrastructures through which they could begin to bridge this gap and continue forward, and because the unions were not yet under sufficient pressure to move. In 2026, a lot has changed. The Left now has three decades of experience since its nadir in the 1990s. Organizations like Sindicato de Inquilinas are the concrete expression of this experience, slowly building power and legitimacy until it can take an occupation of a square, in this case Puerta del Sol, and translate that energy into a bridge to the class. Though an important starting place, how quickly SdI was able to leave the encampment to build the general strike highlights how far we have come since 2011, when the movements were permanently stuck in the squares. On the side of the unions, the economic struggles of their membership push these unions in the opposite direction until their tactics sometimes converge with the movement in the streets. In short, the crisis is presenting renewed opportunities in the current period for reforging the ties neoliberalism severed. Yet this coalescence is far from automatic. It requires that the Left take itself seriously enough to carry out a united strategy to move toward further fraternization between the two now alien camps. This poses some concrete tasks for the Left in the current period, both in the Spanish state and internationally. First, the task of the Left outside of the Spanish state is twofold: To find those struggles through which the Left can create broad and united organizations that can become strong enough to project their legitimacy to the class. Given the universality of precarious housing in the present age, mass tenants organizations pose an interesting possibility for filling this role, especially because of the space they can operate in, right between the economic and the political. For those of us in the unions, we need to continue to push our unions toward the movement, to pressure them from below into united action with the Left on key economic and political questions. I want to be very careful not to exaggerate how far along in this process the comrades in the Spanish state are, but at the same time it’s possible to say that some of the preliminary groundwork has been laid, and the task is somewhat different. Their task is to continue to pull the threads closer and closer together in order to begin to pose the questions of mass, united, and militant action, indefinite general strikes, and eventually social revolution, to make this a legitimate future in people’s minds. By breaking the bonds of movement and class, the neoliberal period also broke the pattern of revolutions started in 1905 by the workers of the Russian Empire. Though the neoliberal age was rife with upheavals and political revolutions, we saw no social revolutions as such. They vanished. Now, neoliberalism in decay may be allowing us to seriously think through the possibility of social revolution on the old model that many had begun to worry was obsolete, of workers stopping production and restarting it again on a new anti-capitalist basis. articles.title: French unions and students fight on as government offers “crumbs”
articles.author: Ana Vračar
articles.content: Nationwide mobilizations against austerity have continued in France following the massive strike on November 5, with additional protests announced for November 10 , 14, 17, and 19. Hundreds of thousands persist in resisting the cuts-based policies envisioned by President Emmanuel Macron and the government of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu. They are demanding that authorities finally table concrete proposals to address the concerns that ignited the protests in October. Read more: 1.6 million join general strike in France against austerity Until now, the Lecornu administration has only offered measures amounting to “crumbs,” according to student organizations and trade unions involved. The latest in this series was a pledge to increase the minimum wage by 1.6%, announced at a meeting with unions and employers on Monday, November 9. “This small increase is not the government’s generosity,” the student union Union Étudiante wrote. “It’s a first step forward made possible by the mobilization of workers, students, trade unions, and everyone who has taken to the streets.” A minimum wage increase worth three metro tickets While government officials claim the increase would help alleviate the cost-of-living crisis plaguing the working class, most trade unions and progressive groups in France have voiced strong disagreement . After factoring in the inflation adjustment already set to kick in from January, the net amount of the government’s promised increase could amount to as little as €7 to €8 net monthly. Trade unions had demanded at least a €100 increase. The government’s offer represents “nothing in the face of precarity,” Union Étudiante emphasized – considering it is just enough to purchase three public transport tickets in Paris or a sandwich in a bakery. “It’s an insult to everyone forced to choose between eating, seeking care, paying rent, and financing their studies,” the student group stated. Protests took place on Tuesday, November 10. Source: Union Étudiante/Facebook “Given the level of the measures announced, the social conference held today at Matignon [the prime minister’s residence] obviously does not put an end to the mobilization,” wrote the General Confederation of Labor (CGT). “On the contrary, it opens a new stage in the balance of power needed to win real progress.” The trade union organization Solidaires similarly criticized the government for failing to offer concrete solutions to the mounting anger, including on student demands for more investment in public education. “The number of additional teachers is insufficient, the funding needed to ensure decent study conditions is nowhere to be seen, and promises on the Parcoursup system remain vague,” they wrote. The left pledges “emergency social decree” to address cost-of-living crisis Student unions that met prime minister Lecornu on Monday shared similar impressions . In addition to noting no significant breakthroughs, students walked out of a discussion on reforming the higher education recruitment platform Parcoursup over the participation of the far right – which has repeatedly dismissed the protesters’ grievances. Most recently, Rassemblement National leader Marine Le Pen opposed imposing a minimum wage increase, arguing it would lead to job losses and echo workplace measures from the USSR. She had previously admitted she would not break with the neoliberalism championed by Macron if elected president in 2027. In contrast, the program of left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon – who is increasingly shaping up to be the only true electoral alternative to Le Pen – pledges to increase the net minimum wage by approximately €200 to €1,700 immediately upon being elected. Jean-Luc Mélenchon and La France Insoumise MPs have supported protests since the beginning. Source: Jean-Luc Mélenchon/Facebook The move would benefit over 2 million workers in France – approximately 60% of whom are women – who were pushed into ultra-precarious working conditions by Macronist policies, wrote media outlet L’Insoumission . “How can we not raise the minimum wage to €1,700 when the wealth of the country’s 500 richest families has doubled since 2017? Billionaires have never made such enormous profits. Macron has turned France into a tax haven for billionaires.” The minimum wage increase promised by the left is among a host of other measures included under the umbrella of an “emergency social decree” intended to address the cost-of-living crisis. Other measures include freezing prices and profit margins, as well as other moves to ensure salaries keep pace with prices. Read more: Dockworkers at 110 ports worldwide strike against war and genocide Students and education trade unions are once again taking action on Tuesday, November 10. On Saturday, November 14, a new round of general mobilizations was announced, while trade unions are circulating a new call to “generalize strike actions” on November 17. Two days later, more protests are expected, boosted by the participation of retirees’ organizations.

articles.title: The financial and political crisis in Paraguay: another sign of the failure of the liberal economic model
articles.author: Thania Saucedo
articles.content: Paraguay is undergoing one of the most significant political and financial crises in its recent history. The Central Bank of Paraguay’s intervention in Ueno Bank – following the detection of serious irregularities in its operations and solvency issues – triggered a crisis that quickly expanded beyond the banking sector. Today, it has direct consequences for the government of Santiago Peña and has triggered an impeachment process that calls into question the very future of the president himself. To understand what is happening, it is necessary to explain a few key points. Ueno Bank experienced exponential growth in recent years, coinciding with the start of Santiago Peña’s administration. It grew to have nearly three million customers (more than 50% of the country’s adult population) and received approximately $800 million in deposits from the public sector. Among these funds are those linked to the Social Security Institute (IPS), which administers the retirement and health contributions of thousands of workers. A massive scam against the people One of the problems is that the president himself maintained business ties with the group associated with the bank until March 2025. Added to this is the fact that Carlos Carvallo, who had served as president of Financiera Ueno, subsequently went on to head the Central Bank, the agency responsible for supervising and regulating the financial system. During this administration, provisions designed to prevent this type of conflict of interest (known as “revolving door” regulations) were also amended. The bank’s intervention, the freezing of deposits, and investigations into loans granted to companies linked to its owners ultimately exposed a web of relationships between private interests and public institutions. However, beyond the numbers and financial transactions, there are thousands of people who today cannot access their savings; workers facing uncertainty about their wages; and retirees whose financial resources are at risk. Financial inclusion, which was touted as one of the great achievements of the economic model, ultimately turned into a massive scam against the population. Read more: Paraguay’s right-wing president resigns as major bank collapses Santiago Peña’s ties to the business group, the decisions made by the executive branch, and the responsibilities of the oversight agencies are among the issues that gave rise to the impeachment request. The opposition spearheaded the process in Congress, and on November 5, the Chamber of Deputies approved the charges against the president. Peña submitted his resignation, but both chambers rejected this attempt to step down, and the Senate proceeded with the process. At the time of this writing, the president is set to present his defense in the impeachment trial. Paraguay’s ruling Colorado Party To understand this crisis, one must also look to the National Republican Association (ANR), the Colorado Party (deeply entrenched in the Paraguayan state apparatus and linked to Alfredo Stroessner’s 35-year dictatorship), and particularly to Horacio Cartes (HC). Paraguay has a political peculiarity that is fundamental to understanding what is happening. The Colorado Party has governed virtually uninterrupted since 1947; the only interruption in that long cycle was the administration of Fernando Lugo (2008–2012), who came to power leading an alliance that managed to defeat the Colorado Party at the polls after more than six decades. However, his administration came to an abrupt end in June 2012 through a parliamentary coup that removed him from office in just 48 hours via a controversial impeachment trial. For social movements and sectors of the popular base, this event was not just another episode in history but a political operation orchestrated by sectors of the Paraguayan right, with Horacio Cartes as one of its main actors and with alleged complicity and support from external interests, including those of the U.S. Embassy. Currently, power within the ANR is fiercely contested by internal factions, but the Cartes faction (HC) has become the ruling party’s main power base. Cartes was not only president of the Republic from 2013 to 2018 but subsequently assumed the presidency of the Colorado Party itself and maintained enormous influence over the decisions of Santiago Peña’s government. Peña rose to the presidency with Cartes’ political backing. His candidacy and subsequent administration were built under the leadership of the Honor Colorado movement. For this reason, what we are seeing today involves a major political contradiction: the very same faction that built and sustained this administration has now decided to support the impeachment proceedings against the president. Cartes’ position shifted as the crisis unfolded. Initially, his inner circle rejected the possibility of impeachment and sought to pin the blame on Central Bank officials. However, on November 5, Cartes publicly announced that the ANR would support Peña’s impeachment. This move cannot be interpreted simply as an institutional decision by the Colorado Party; it also reflects a struggle for political control, for the continuity of the government’s agenda, and for the preservation of a power structure that the movement itself helped build. A systemic failure of free market capitalism Against this backdrop, social movements and the popular sector are not limiting their criticism to demanding individual accountability and rejecting any attempt at impunity; they are also warning that this crisis is yet another example of the failure of the liberal economic model, which for years insisted that the market could regulate itself, that the state should reduce its intervention, and that privatization and deregulation were the path to development. They promised that, if we let capital operate freely, wealth would eventually reach the entire population, that economic growth would translate into well-being, and that everyone would benefit from this supposed trickle-down effect. In Paraguay today, the consequences are felt by every worker, as a result of financial narco-capitalism. This is a model that unscrupulously manages public resources, concentrates wealth, and fosters ties between political power and private interests. It is a system in which profits remain in the hands of certain sectors, while the consequences of their operations ultimately fall on the population. Therefore, what is happening on this side of the southern part of our America is not isolated from what is happening in other parts of the world; it is part of a dynamic in which big capital dictates political decisions, appropriates the commons, and turns basic rights and needs into business opportunities. The settings change, the actors change, but the logic remains the same. However, the evident failure of the economic policy of financial capitalism also opens up an opportunity for the organized popular movement: to envision a different future and build a political and economic alternative that breaks with this logic – to pave the way toward a world in which the economy serves life rather than the accumulation of wealth by a few, and in which people can decide on their resources, their present, and their destiny. Thania Saucedo is a journalist and political leader with the Frente Guasu in Paraguay. This article was produced by Globetrotter .

articles.title: Millions of IDPs in Sudan in need of emergency shelter as winter approaches, UN warns
articles.author: Pavan Kulkarni
articles.content: Millions forced to flee their homes by the ongoing war in Sudan “risk being left without a roof over their heads,” the UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM) warned on November 6. 15.4 million people are in urgent need of “emergency shelter and essential household items.” However, humanitarian agencies have only provided assistance to 936,000 people, which is just over 6% of those in need. “Funding constraints mean humanitarian agencies can prioritize assistance for just 10% of those in need,” the agencies said in a joint statement. ​As the war continues in its fourth year, 8.6 million people remain displaced within Sudan, while 4.6 million have fled across the borders to neighboring countries. ​ Although 5.2 million have returned to their original areas, their homes are damaged in the fighting. So are essential services and infrastructure in their areas. They are left with “little or nothing to rebuild their lives,” the joint statement said.​ “The loss of shelter in Sudan is no longer merely one of the consequences of the war. It has become a humanitarian crisis threatening the lives of millions of people and depriving displaced families of the most basic conditions of safety and stability,” said Adam Rojal, spokesperson of the General Coordination of Displaced Persons and Refugees Camps. Lack of clean water and healthcare is worsening their condition, posing particular risks to children, the elderly, and women, he added.​ “And now winter is approaching,” said Abubakr Jalloh, UNHCR’s Deputy Representative in Sudan. “Sudan is known as a country of extreme heat. That is true. Yet winter nights in Darfur can be bitterly cold, and the temperatures in northern Sudan can fall to single digits. For newborn babies or older persons, a blanket can be a life-saving item.” ​However, even the provision of blankets to those in need is a challenge as Sudan’s 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan has received less than half the required funding. Insisting that “displaced persons and refugees are rights-holders, not merely recipients of relief,” Rojal said that their participation should be ensured in determining how international agencies prioritize humanitarian response. ​ “Behind every family without shelter lies a story of loss and suffering, and behind every child sleeping without a roof over their head is a threatened future. This suffering must not become normalized or reduced to mere figures in international reports.” Read more: The war in Sudan is “between two wings of a comprador parasitic capitalist class”

articles.title: Pentagon Whistleblower Wes Bryant: Impeach Hegseth. He’s a “Clear & Present Danger” to Democracy
articles.content: This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form. AMY GOODMAN : The House is moving towards a vote this week on whether to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth. The outgoing Republican Congressmember Thomas Massie of Kentucky introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday for violating the Constitution and ignoring the will of Congress. REP . THOMAS MASSIE : Wherefore, Secretary of Defense Peter Hegseth, by such conduct, has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties and the rule of law. Peter Brian Hegseth thus warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States. Because we tore down their sacred cows, one by one and without apology. DEI is a Marxist ideology built to destroy us, so we crushed it. … Patriot extremism, it’s not a thing. Patriots are now in control. Being trans is a mental illness incompatible with military service. … Military bases should not be renamed in the name of understanding “white rage.” … Narcoterrorists should die, not be caught and released. … Sealing the border and mass deportations are military functions. And when we say that Iran will not have a nuclear weapon, we actually mean it. … We will stand. We will fight. And we will defend this republic from all enemies, foreign and domestic. AMY GOODMAN : President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio say they’re standing by Hegseth. Trump spoke to reporters Sunday. PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP : A lot of people agree. WES BRYANT : Right, exactly. This is just incredibly shameful. These so-called narcoterrorism strikes have been shown to be, you know, by both current and former military lawyers and other government lawyers, State Department, for example, to be completely illegal, out of accordance with U.S. law and especially with international law. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And can you also elaborate on Hegseth’s lethality doctrine, his Christian nationalist views, and why you see him as fundamentally unfit? WES BRYANT : Right. You combine this with his fixation on hypermasculinity, which, frankly, is reminiscent of the Aryan movement of the Third Reich, what Hitler’s Nazi Germany called the “new German man,” and now you have this amalgamation of worldview and outlook combined with an application into the operational use of the U.S. military that becomes just an outlook of killing and destruction, and a reveling in and glorification of war. Then you have his disdain, you know, his blatant, overt disdain, for rules of engagement, Geneva Conventions, the laws of war. And now you combine all of this together, and along with weak and complicit military command, and it’s no wonder that we have atrocities being carried out, that we have all of these illegal wars and operations being carried out. When you look at these articles of impeachment — violating the War Powers Resolution, ignoring laws that minimize civilian casualties, these extrajudicial killings in the Caribbean and the Pacific — ultimately, this is President Trump who’s ordering this, and he’s carrying out his orders, isn’t he? WES BRYANT : Absolutely. You know, Hegseth should be the first domino. But, you know, I think the reality here is that Hegseth is the first and most realistic target, so we need to pursue removing him. And, you know, I, for one, would be more than willing to lead that charge. And then let’s go after Trump and the rest of the administration following. AMY GOODMAN : And the not minimizing civilian casualties — the unit actually that you were chief of, the civilian harm assessment at the Pentagon, you did that for a year. Are we talking about both in the case of Iran, Iranians, like the children in Minab, when the U.S. — it looks overwhelmingly that the evidence is the U.S. bombed the girls’ school in southern Iran; the Pentagon hasn’t come out with a report on this, though they said they were going to — but also U.S. troops and civilians in the area of the Gulf when they waged war on Iran, all of these bases where Americans were wounded? But start with the Iranians and what this unit for civilian harm assessment was that was shut down in the Pentagon. WES BRYANT : Yeah, you know, the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Enterprise consisted of a few hundred individuals, spread across the Pentagon and the combatant commands, that were there to do exactly this. You know, if they had been emplaced at the Central Command, for example, if those personnel had been overseeing the strike planning for every single target set in Iran, I promise that a strike as egregious of a failure as Minab would not have happened. And then you have the detractions, the devolutions of operational practice and standards in general, where, you know, even aside from my unit that existed, the Civilian Harm Enterprise, the U.S. military has been violating standing doctrine and practices in targeting and civilian harm mitigation that even existed over the course of the past 20, 30 years. You know, you combine this with Hegseth’s deemphasis on the protection of civilian, his glorification of and reveling in war and violence, his direction — his directives to carry out mass bombing campaigns, and what I believe is his directives that he’s making, you know, over secured lines or in secured areas to the commanders themselves, so that they’re unrecorded, to actually have a higher tolerance for civilian casualties. We’ve got this incredible spike in civilian casualties, not just Minab in Iran. It’s upwards of 3,000-plus potential civilians killed, along with, you know, massive destruction of civilian infrastructure, even targeting of cultural heritage sites, hospitals, schools — more than just Minab — police and fire entities, vital energy infrastructure. So, it’s incredible, what we’re seeing, this devolution of the U.S. military under Hegseth. JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Wes Bryant, I’m wondering: During the period of the Biden administration, did you encounter in your — in that unit particularly glaring attacks that affected civilians that may not have gotten much attention? WES BRYANT : No, you know, I wouldn’t say so. Most of the — you know, we’ve had, obviously, civilian harm incidents in the past. Look at the withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021, where the U.S. struck an aid worker and children, his family. You know, that was one of the catalysts to kickstart the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Enterprise. You have — going back before that, you have some instances in the fights against ISIS in Mosul, Raqqa. You have the 2015 very tragic strike against a MSF hospital, a Doctors Without Borders hospital, in Afghanistan. And, you know, what we were doing under the Civilian Harm Mitigation and Response Enterprise, and collectively, as a joint force, at all the combatant commands, was doing a really hard look back up through the Biden administration of what the U.S. did right during the “war on terror,” and all of the various failures and how we could improve those. And we had some pretty fantastic momentum, and that was all at full stop under this Hegseth regime. And we’ve devolved even past that. You know, we’ve gone back decades, frankly, in our application of precision, in our ability and, really, willingness to safeguard the innocent and carry out the war with humanity and honor, and to have accountability and transparency when failures happen. We see no transparency and the opposite of accountability from the Hegseth regime. I mean, he truly operates like a fascist military dictator — you know, totalitarian control and extremist nationalism and a hypermilitarism. articles.title: “We Have to Be Brave”: Palestinian Journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh Speaks Out After Israeli Detention
articles.content: The prominent journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, a Palestinian citizen of Israel, has been released from Israeli custody after five days in detention. He was arrested on Wednesday by armed police and Shin Bet agents who conducted a nighttime raid on his home in the Israeli city of Jaffa. Abu Shehadeh’s detention was related to his reporting on the October 27 Israeli election and the role of Palestinian political parties. Ahead of the election, he interviewed Azmi Bishara, a Palestinian intellectual and former member of the Israeli Knesset who has lived in exile in Qatar since fleeing Israel amid allegations that he aided Hezbollah during the 2006 Lebanon war. Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of “contacting a foreign agent,” in connection to his interview with Bishara. “Men with ski masks knock on your door at 11 at night. They tell you that they have an arrest warrant. They raid the house. They wake your wife, your children,” says Shehadeh. “It tells how messianic and dangerous the extreme right in Israel has become, willing to use this unprecedented power against journalists.”

articles.title: Will Lawrence, Sunrise Movement Co-Founder, Elected to Congress on Anti-Data Center Platform
articles.content: Progressive candidate Will Lawrence of Michigan has defeated Republican incumbent Tom Barrett, flipping the state’s 7th Congressional District, a closely watched swing district that includes Lansing. Lawrence, the co-founder of the youth-led climate organization Sunrise Movement, refused corporate PAC money, instead building a people-powered grassroots mobilization campaign. He focused on lowering the costs of housing and healthcare, opposing the war on Iran, and challenging the power of Big Tech. “I’m fighting for a federal moratorium on new data center development, along with a pause on advanced AI development,” says Lawrence. “These developers come into small towns, and they say, ’We’re going to suck up a bunch of water. We’re going to use more energy than the current capacity of the grid. We don’t know what’s going to happen to your property values, but if everything goes well, we’re going to put 10 or 20 million people out of work, and if it goes poorly, we may kill everybody by accident.’” Lawrence also says he will back Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, but that he will demand Democratic leadership listen to progressive concerns.
